idiom_name: behaviour struct/enum + a render closure (impl Fn(&State) -> R); framework children props as FnOnce
implementation_notes: Rust carries the pattern with ordinary generic closures: the behaviour is a struct or state enum exposing view(&self, markup: impl FnOnce(&Self) -> R) -> R, so the consumer chooses what to produce while the state machine stays owned and testable - the language needs no render-prop machinery because closures are values that capture their environment. In component frameworks the same shape appears as children props: Yew keeps parent-to-child communication in reference-counted Properties passed down the tree, and children are simply another prop; Leptos renders closures (Fn() -> T implements IntoView) and its control-flow components take closures as children. What replaces the classic structure is the closure parameter; keep the state machine free of widget types so one logic backs several views, and reach for an immediate-mode GUI when the frame function owning the state is simpler than a retained tree.
pitfalls: Choosing Fn/FnMut/FnOnce and where the state is borrowed: a render closure that calls back into the behaviour conflicts with the immutable borrow - model input as messages/events instead of &mut callbacks.
Trait objects (dyn) erase the render type and force boxing; prefer generics until the type explosion is worse than an allocation.
Rc<RefCell<_>> state panics at runtime if the render callback re-enters while a borrow is active.
Framework children props are shared immutable snapshots, so mutable interaction state must live in signals/stores rather than in the props passed down.
